chains.title: The RBA raises the cash rate
chains.reverse: The RBA cuts the cash rate
chains.trigger: The RBA Monetary Policy Board raises its cash rate target to bring inflation back to the 2–3% target band.

stem.why: The Board lifts its target for the interest rate on overnight loans between banks.

stem.v: Market interest rates on loans and deposits
stem.why: Banks' funding costs rise, so they pass the increase on to mortgages, business loans and savings accounts.

links.v: Cost of borrowing and reward for saving
links.why: Credit is dearer and saving earns more, so households and firms have a reason to spend less now.
Households put off spending, especially on items bought with credit such as cars and renovations.
Fewer projects earn enough to cover the higher cost of borrowing.
Lenders raise the rates on existing loans, so required repayments increase.
More of each pay goes to the bank. Savers earn more interest, but households in total owe more than they hold in deposits.
With less left over after repayments, indebted households cut back.
Buyers can borrow less, and safer interest-bearing assets now look more attractive.
Weaker demand lowers asset prices, or slows their growth.
Households that feel less wealthy spend less: the wealth effect.

links.v: Return on Australian assets compared with overseas
links.why: Australian interest rates rise relative to those in other countries.
Foreign investors buy Australian dollars to earn the higher return.
More demand for the currency causes an appreciation.
Exports become less competitive and imports cheaper. Cheaper imports also lower inflation directly.

tail.why: Consumption, investment and net exports are all weaker.
Firms cut production as spending slows.
Firms need fewer workers, so spare capacity opens up in the labour market.
Weaker demand and slower wages growth give firms less room to raise prices.

chains.lag: Interest rates change quickly, but the full effect on inflation can take one to two years.
limits: It works on demand. It cannot remove inflation that comes from supply shocks, such as higher oil prices.
Fixed-rate loans and savings buffers delay the cash flow channel.
It is a blunt tool: borrowers and interest-sensitive industries such as housing bear most of the cost.
The exchange rate channel depends on what other central banks do with their rates.
If people expect high inflation to continue, wages and prices keep rising for longer.
chains.diagram: AD–AS diagram: AD shifts left from AD to AD₁, so the price level and real GDP both fall.

chains.title: The government runs an expansionary budget
chains.reverse: The government runs a contractionary budget
chains.trigger: The Australian Government raises its spending or cuts taxes to lift economic activity.

stem.why: Discretionary decisions raise spending or lower revenue, so the budget moves towards deficit.

links.why: Spending on infrastructure, services or payments is an injection into the circular flow.

links.v: Output and employment in supplying firms
links.why: Firms that win the work produce more and hire more workers.
Households keep more of their pay or receive larger payments.
Part of the extra income is spent and part is saved. The share spent is the marginal propensity to consume.

tail.why: G and C are both components of AD = C + I + G + (X − M).
One person's spending is another's income, so the first increase is multiplied: k = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC).
Firms raise production to meet the extra demand.
Demand for labour is derived from demand for goods and services.
If the economy is near full capacity, extra demand pulls prices up.

chains.lag: There is an implementation lag: budgets are annual and most measures need legislation. Once the money is spent, the effect is fairly fast.
limits: Some of the extra income leaks into saving, tax and imports, which weakens the multiplier and widens the current account deficit.
Government borrowing can push up interest rates and crowd out private investment.
Deficits add to public debt, which limits what future budgets can do.
When inflation is high, stimulus works against the RBA's monetary policy.
Political constraints: spending is easy to start and hard to withdraw.
chains.diagram: AD–AS diagram: AD shifts right from AD to AD₁, so real GDP and the price level both rise.

chains.title: The Australian dollar depreciates
chains.short: A fall in the exchange rate
chains.trigger: The value of the Australian dollar falls against other currencies.

links.v: Price of Australian exports in foreign currency
links.why: Overseas buyers need less of their own currency to buy the same Australian goods and services.
Australian goods and services are cheaper than rival products.
Overseas buyers purchase more, and tourists and students find Australia cheaper.
Exports are an injection, so growth and employment rise.

links.v: Price of imports in Australian dollars
links.why: Each Australian dollar buys less foreign currency.
Households and firms switch to local substitutes where they can.
Local producers win sales from dearer imports.

links.v: Cost of imported goods and inputs
links.why: Fuel, machinery and consumer goods priced in foreign currency cost more in Australian dollars.
Firms pass higher import costs on to consumers, raising the CPI.
Wages buy less when prices rise faster than pay.

links.v: Australian-dollar value of debt owed in foreign currencies
links.why: The same foreign-currency debt converts into more Australian dollars: the valuation effect.
Interest payments in foreign currency take more Australian dollars.
Larger interest payments are debits on the current account.

chains.overall: A depreciation helps exporters and import-competing firms but raises inflation and the cost of foreign debt.
chains.lag: Volumes respond slowly. The current account can worsen at first because import bills rise before export volumes do: the J-curve.
limits: The gain depends on how responsive buyers are to price. Commodity exports are priced in US dollars and limited by supply.
Firms that rely on imported inputs face higher costs, which offsets their competitive gain.
If the depreciation was caused by lower commodity prices, the loss of export income can outweigh the benefit.
Higher imported inflation may lead the RBA to raise interest rates.
chains.diagram: Market for the Australian dollar: the supply of A$ shifts right (or demand shifts left), so the exchange rate falls from ER to ER₁.

chains.title: Commodity prices fall
chains.short: A fall in the terms of trade
chains.trigger: World prices for Australia's main exports, such as iron ore, coal and gas, fall.

stem.why: Export prices fall relative to import prices, so a given volume of exports buys fewer imports.

links.why: The same volume of exports earns less.
Export credits fall while import debits are unchanged.
A smaller trade surplus moves the current account towards deficit.
Overseas buyers need fewer Australian dollars to pay for exports.
Lower demand for the currency causes a depreciation.
The lower dollar helps farmers, manufacturers, tourism and education. The floating exchange rate acts as a shock absorber.
Resource companies earn less for each tonne sold.
Lower prices make new projects less profitable.
Lower profits mean less tax collected.
Revenue falls short of forecasts, so the deficit widens or the surplus shrinks.

tail.why: Australia earns less from the rest of the world for the same work, so living standards grow more slowly.

chains.lag: The exchange rate reacts within days. Investment, jobs and the budget take months to years.
limits: The depreciation offsets part of the income loss.
Export volumes may rise as earlier mining investment comes into production.
The size of the effect depends on how much of Australia's export base is commodities.
Global influences are outside the control of Australian policy.
chains.diagram: Market for the Australian dollar: demand for A$ shifts left, so the exchange rate falls from ER to ER₁.

chains.title: Australia cuts its tariffs
chains.trigger: The Australian Government lowers or removes tariffs on imported goods.

stem.why: The tax on imports is lower, so the landed price falls towards the world price.

strands.name: Consumers and firms that use imports

links.why: Imports are cheaper, and local firms must match them.
Imported machinery and components cost less.
The same income buys more, and inflation is lower.
Local producers lose the price advantage the tariff gave them.

links.v: Output of less efficient local firms
links.why: Firms that cannot match the world price lose sales or close.
Workers in those industries and regions lose jobs, and their skills may not match the jobs available.

links.v: Resources moving to industries with a comparative advantage
links.why: Labour and capital shift to where Australia produces at a lower opportunity cost.
Competition forces firms to cut costs and innovate.
More efficient firms with cheaper inputs can sell more overseas.
A lower rate is collected on each import.

chains.overall: The costs are immediate and fall on particular industries and regions. The gains are spread widely and build over time.
chains.lag: Prices fall quickly. The shift of resources into more efficient industries takes years.
limits: Adjustment costs are concentrated, so displaced workers need retraining and support.
Other countries may keep their own protection, so Australian exporters do not gain equal access.
Some industries may be kept for strategic or security reasons.
Political constraints: the workers who lose are easy to see and the consumers who gain are not.
chains.diagram: Tariff diagram: the price falls from Pw+t to Pw. Domestic output falls, consumption rises and imports increase.

chains.title: Wages grow faster than productivity
chains.reverse: Wages grow more slowly than productivity
chains.trigger: Nominal wages rise faster than output per worker.

links.why: Firms pay more for each unit of output because pay has risen faster than output per worker.
Firms raise prices to protect their profit margins.
Higher costs of production shift aggregate supply to the left.
Workers expect higher prices and seek higher pay again: the wage–price spiral.
Workers take home more pay.
Most of the extra income is spent.
If the economy is near capacity, the extra spending pulls prices up.

links.v: Cost of labour compared with capital
links.why: Workers become more expensive relative to machines and software.
Firms substitute capital for labour or hire fewer workers.
Australian costs rise relative to those of trading partners.
Fewer jobs are offered at the higher wage, especially for low-skilled workers.

chains.overall: Wage rises are sustainable when matched by productivity. When they are not, they add to inflation and can cost jobs.
chains.lag: Wage decisions flow through over one to two years as awards and enterprise agreements are renewed.
limits: If productivity grows as fast as wages, unit labour costs do not rise.
Firms may absorb higher wages in lower profit margins instead of raising prices.
After a period of falling real wages, a rise may only restore lost purchasing power.
The RBA may raise the cash rate if wages growth threatens the inflation target.
chains.diagram: AD–AS diagram: AS shifts left from AS to AS₁, so the price level rises and real GDP falls.

chains.title: Growth slows in Australia's major trading partners
chains.reverse: Growth picks up in Australia's major trading partners
chains.trigger: Economic growth falls in economies such as China, Japan and the United States.

links.why: Trading partners with lower incomes buy fewer resources, services and manufactured goods.
Weaker world demand lowers both the quantity sold and its price.
Lower prices and volumes cut what exporters earn.
Bad news from overseas and falling share prices make firms and households cautious.
Firms delay projects and households save more.
In a downturn investors move funds to safe assets such as US government bonds.
Less capital inflow and lower commodity prices reduce demand for the currency.
The lower dollar cushions exporters and import-competing firms.

tail.why: Exports, investment and consumption are all weaker.
The Australian business cycle follows the international business cycle.
Firms need fewer workers when demand falls.
Automatic stabilisers: tax revenue falls and welfare payments rise without any new decision.

chains.lag: Share prices and the dollar react at once. Exports, jobs and the budget follow over the next few quarters.
limits: Expansionary monetary and fiscal policy can offset part of the fall in demand.
The floating exchange rate absorbs some of the shock.
The effect depends on which trading partner slows: China matters most for resource exports.
Global influences limit what domestic policy can achieve.
chains.diagram: AD–AS diagram: AD shifts left. Or the business cycle: Australia moving from an upswing into a downswing.

chains.title: Productivity rises
chains.trigger: Microeconomic reform, new technology or better skills raise output per unit of input.

stem.why: Firms produce more from the same labour and capital.

links.why: Competition pushes firms to pass lower costs on to buyers.
The economy can grow without the same pressure on prices.
Australian goods and services become cheaper relative to rivals.
Local firms win sales at home and overseas.
A stronger trade balance improves the current account.

links.v: Firms' capacity to pay higher wages
links.why: Each worker produces more, so higher pay does not raise unit labour costs.
Wages can rise faster than prices.

tail.why: The economy's productive capacity grows: the AS curve shifts right.
The economy can grow faster without causing inflation.

chains.lag: Long. The benefits of reform can take many years to appear.
limits: Time lags: governments bear the political cost long before the gains arrive.
Reform causes structural unemployment in the short run as inefficient firms close.
The gains may go to profits instead of wages or lower prices if markets are not competitive.
Political constraints: the groups that lose from reform resist it.
chains.diagram: AD–AS diagram: AS shifts right from AS to AS₁, so real GDP rises and the price level falls.

chains.title: Inflation rises above the target band
chains.trigger: The general level of prices rises faster than the RBA's 2–3% target.

links.why: Prices rise faster than most pay packets.
The same income buys fewer goods and services.
People on low or fixed incomes spend most of their income on essentials and are hit hardest.
Money in the bank buys less each year unless interest rates keep up.
Borrowers repay with dollars that are worth less, so wealth shifts from lenders to borrowers.

links.v: Australian prices compared with trading partners
links.why: Local costs and prices rise faster than those overseas.
Exports are dearer and imports relatively cheaper.
Export volumes fall and import volumes rise.
People come to expect that prices will keep rising.
Workers seek pay rises to cover expected inflation.
The RBA tightens monetary policy to return inflation to target.
Higher interest rates slow spending, and unemployment rises.

chains.overall: High inflation redistributes income, erodes competitiveness and forces a policy response that slows growth.
chains.lag: Real incomes fall straight away. The policy response and its effect on growth follow over one to two years.
limits: The effect on households depends on whether wages and welfare payments are indexed to prices.
Borrowers gain only if interest rates do not rise by as much as inflation.
If trading partners have similar inflation, competitiveness is little changed.
Low, stable inflation is the aim. Deflation carries costs of its own.
chains.diagram: Phillips curve, or AD–AS showing the cause: AD shifting right (demand-pull) or AS shifting left (cost-push).

chains.title: Australia runs a current account deficit year after year
chains.trigger: Payments to the rest of the world on the current account exceed receipts for many years.

stem.why: A current account deficit must be funded by borrowing from overseas or selling assets to foreign investors.

links.why: Each year's borrowing adds to the stock of debt.
A larger debt costs more to service.
Interest payments are debits on the current account.
The deficit feeds itself: the debt trap.
Foreign investors buy shares, companies and property.
Owners take their returns out of Australia.
Dividends are also debits on the current account.
Australia needs a steady inflow of funds to cover the gap.

links.v: Exposure to changes in investor confidence
links.why: If lenders lose confidence they demand higher returns or withdraw funds.

links.v: Risk of a sharp depreciation and higher interest rates
links.why: A sudden fall in capital inflow lowers the dollar and raises the cost of borrowing.
Foreign saving lets Australia invest more than it saves.
Investment in mines, infrastructure and technology expands what the economy can produce.
The extra output can service the debt. On this view a deficit from private decisions is not a problem: the Pitchford thesis.

chains.overall: A current account deficit is sustainable when the borrowing funds productive investment and lenders stay confident.
chains.lag: The stock of liabilities builds slowly, but a loss of confidence can happen within days.
limits: Most foreign debt is private, taken on by firms and banks that expect to repay it.
Much of the debt is hedged or in Australian dollars, which reduces the valuation risk.
A floating exchange rate adjusts gradually, which lowers the chance of a crisis.
The debt servicing ratio shows whether export income can cover the interest.
chains.diagram: Flow chart of the debt trap cycle: CAD → foreign borrowing → net foreign debt → interest payments → net primary income deficit → CAD.

chains.title: A price is put on carbon emissions
chains.trigger: The government makes polluters pay for each tonne of greenhouse gas they emit, through a tax or tradable permits.

stem.why: The external cost of pollution is added to the firm's own costs: the externality is internalised.

links.why: Higher costs shift the supply curve to the left.
Firms pass on part of the cost.
Buyers respond to the higher price.
Less of the polluting good is made.

links.v: Cost of clean technology compared with polluting technology
links.why: Renewables and energy efficiency become relatively cheaper.
Firms have a lasting incentive to cut the emissions they must pay for.
Production methods change, not only the quantity produced.
Electricity and gas producers pass on the carbon cost.
Low-income households spend a larger share of income on energy, so the effect is regressive.

links.v: Costs compared with overseas rivals that face no carbon price
links.why: Australian producers pay a cost their competitors do not.
Exports and import-competing firms lose sales.
Emissions shift to another country instead of falling: carbon leakage.

chains.overall: A carbon price cuts emissions at the lowest cost to the economy, but raises prices and needs compensation and international co-operation.
chains.lag: Prices change at once. Investment in new technology takes years.
limits: Political constraints: higher energy prices are unpopular, and policy has changed with governments.
Carbon leakage, unless other countries act or trade-exposed firms are shielded.
Demand for energy is not very responsive to price in the short run.
Climate change is a global problem, so one country's action has limited effect alone.
chains.diagram: Negative externality diagram: the carbon price lifts the private cost curve (MPC) up to the social cost curve (MSC), so output falls to the socially efficient level.

chains.title: Unemployment rises
chains.trigger: The unemployment rate increases as the economy slows.

links.v: Number of people producing goods and services
links.why: Workers who want jobs are idle.

links.v: Real GDP compared with its potential
links.why: The economy operates inside its production possibility frontier. The lost output is an opportunity cost.
Wages are replaced by much lower welfare payments.
Unemployed households spend less, and employed households save more in case they are next.
Lower spending leads firms to cut more jobs: a downward multiplier.
Fewer people earn taxable income.
More people qualify for JobSeeker.
These automatic stabilisers widen the deficit without any new decision.
The longer people are out of work, the harder it is to return.
Skills and work habits fade, so cyclical unemployment can become structural.
Income losses fall on particular groups and regions, with poorer health and family stress.

links.v: Spare capacity in the labour market
links.why: More people compete for each job.
Workers have less bargaining power.
Slower growth in labour costs and weaker demand ease price pressure.

chains.overall: Unemployment wastes resources, widens the budget deficit and inequality, and eases inflation.
chains.lag: Jobs are lost quickly in a downturn. Long-term unemployment and skill loss last for years after growth returns.
limits: The costs depend on how long people stay unemployed, not only on the unemployment rate.
Underemployment and hidden unemployment mean the rate understates the spare capacity.
Welfare payments and automatic stabilisers cushion the fall in consumption.
Below the NAIRU, lower unemployment adds to inflation, which is a conflict between objectives.
chains.diagram: AD–AS diagram: AD shifts left and real GDP falls below full-employment output. Or a production possibility frontier with a point inside it.
